Supply chain ethics is irrelevant as long as the company complies with minimum legal requirements

questionText: Which of the following BEST describes how a company should approach "supply chain strategy execution" to ensure strategies are effectively implemented?
options: Publishing the strategy document and assuming implementation will follow automatically

Translating supply chain strategy into specific operational initiatives with clear ownership, resource allocation, timelines, and measurable milestones; building implementation capability through change management; establishing governance mechanisms to track progress and address barriers; and creating a culture of execution accountability where supply chain teams are empowered and motivated to deliver strategic outcomes
Delegating all strategy execution to external consultants
Waiting for the strategy to be proven successful by competitors before implementing it

questionText: Which of the following represents a fundamental limitation of traditional supply chain strategic planning approaches in an era of rapid disruption?
options: Traditional planning approaches are too focused on cost reduction

Traditional annual planning cycles and deterministic forecasting assumptions are insufficient in an era of rapid, unpredictable change — companies need more dynamic strategic planning capabilities including scenario planning, real-time environmental sensing, rapid strategy adjustment mechanisms, and organizational agility to execute strategic pivots when required
Traditional planning approaches are too technology-intensive
Traditional planning approaches focus too much on customer requirements

questionText: A company is designing its supply chain strategy for the next five years. Which mega-trend should receive the MOST strategic attention?
options: Short-term fluctuations in transportation fuel prices

The convergence of digital transformation, sustainability imperatives, supply chain regionalization trends, and changing consumer expectations — which together are fundamentally restructuring supply chain competitive dynamics and requiring companies to simultaneously invest in digital capabilities, sustainable practices, resilient network designs, and customer-centric fulfillment models
Annual changes in academic supply chain research priorities
Short-term changes in currency exchange rates

questionText: Evaluate how "supply chain transparency" creates strategic value beyond compliance and risk management:
options: Transparency only creates value by reducing regulatory compliance risk

Transparency creates strategic value by building consumer trust and brand equity, enabling premium pricing for ethically sourced products, strengthening supplier relationships through open information sharing, facilitating faster problem identification and resolution, supporting data-driven strategic decision-making, and increasingly differentiating companies in markets where consumers, investors, and regulators demand evidence of responsible and sustainable supply chain practices
Transparency only matters for companies selling directly to consumers
Transparency creates no strategic value and should only be pursued when legally required

questionText: Which of the following BEST describes the concept of "supply chain as a competitive weapon" in strategic management?
options: Using legal tactics to prevent competitors from accessing key suppliers

Developing supply chain capabilities — such as superior delivery speed, inventory efficiency, cost structure, product customization ability, or supply chain resilience — that create customer value and market differentiation that competitors cannot easily or quickly replicate, making the supply chain itself a primary source of sustained competitive advantage
Using supply chain disruptions to harm competitor operations
Filing patents on supply chain processes to prevent competitor imitation

questionText: A logistics and supply chain graduate in Ethiopia aspiring to become a supply chain strategist should prioritize developing which combination of competencies?
options: Only technical logistics operations skills

A combination of strategic thinking and analytical capabilities (environmental analysis, strategic frameworks, quantitative modeling), deep supply chain domain knowledge (network design, sourcing strategy, operations management), digital literacy (supply chain technology, data analytics), Ethiopian and regional market context understanding, and relationship and leadership skills needed to drive strategic supply chain initiatives across organizational boundaries
Only financial and accounting skills
Only negotiation and contract management skills

questionText: Which of the following BEST describes the concept of "supply chain ambidexterity"?
options: The ability to manage two different transportation modes simultaneously

The organizational capability to simultaneously pursue operational efficiency in the current supply chain while investing in exploration and innovation for future supply chain capabilities — balancing the exploitation of existing supply chain assets and practices with the development of new capabilities needed for future competitive success
Using both manual and automated processes in warehouse operations
Managing supply chains in two different geographic regions simultaneously

questionText: A company is evaluating whether to adopt a "platform-based supply chain" model. Which strategic consideration is MOST critical?
options: Whether the platform has an attractive user interface design

Whether the platform model creates sufficient network effects and ecosystem value to justify the investment and strategic transformation required, whether the company has the digital capabilities and partner relationships to build or join a successful platform, and whether platform participation enhances or compromises the company's competitive position
Whether competitors are already using platform-based supply chains
Whether the platform is compatible with the company's existing email system

questionText: Analyze the strategic supply chain implications of "consumer power shift" driven by digital channels and social media:
options: Consumer power shift has no supply chain implications

The shift of power to consumers through digital channels creates supply chain imperatives for greater transparency, faster fulfillment, higher personalization, seamless returns processing, and real-time order visibility — requiring supply chains to become more customer-centric, responsive, and transparent, with fulfillment capabilities that match rising consumer expectations shaped by best-in-class e-commerce experiences
Consumer power shift only affects marketing strategies
Consumer power shift reduces the complexity of supply chain management

questionText: Which of the following BEST evaluates the strategic adequacy of a supply chain that performs well on cost metrics but poorly on resilience metrics?
options: The supply chain is strategically adequate because cost efficiency is the primary goal

The supply chain is strategically inadequate for volatile operating environments — its cost efficiency may be eroded or destroyed by a single significant disruption that it lacks the resilience to absorb or recover from quickly; strategic adequacy requires balancing efficiency with sufficient resilience to protect the revenue, customer relationships, and market position that the efficient supply chain is designed to serve
The supply chain only needs resilience improvements if a major disruption occurs
Resilience metrics are irrelevant as long as cost metrics meet targets

questionText: Evaluate the strategic significance of Ethiopia's geographic position as a potential logistics hub for East Africa:
options: Ethiopia's landlocked geography is exclusively a disadvantage with no strategic significance

Ethiopia's central geographic position in East Africa, combined with investments in industrial parks, Addis Ababa's role as a major African aviation hub, expanding road and rail infrastructure, and growing regional economic integration, creates strategic opportunities to develop supply chain capabilities that serve both the domestic market and broader regional and continental trade — making supply chain investment in Ethiopia potentially valuable not just for the local market but as a platform for East African regional supply chain operations
Ethiopia's geography is only relevant for transportation companies
Ethiopia's strategic geographic position has no implications for supply chain strategy

questionText: A supply chain strategist is evaluating the long-term strategic implications of increasing automation in supply chain operations. Which consideration is MOST important from a strategic perspective?
options: How automation affects the number of forklifts needed in warehouses

How automation reshapes the competitive dynamics of the industry — potentially lowering barriers to achieving supply chain cost efficiency (reducing traditional cost advantages of low-wage locations), changing the skills mix required in supply chain talent, enabling new levels of supply chain speed and precision, and creating new competitive differentiation possibilities through superior automation capabilities
Whether automation is cheaper than manual operations in the short term
Whether automation is technically feasible in the company's existing warehouses

questionText: Which of the following BEST describes the concept of "supply chain strategy as emergent process" in strategic management theory?
options: Supply chains develop their strategies randomly without planning

Supply chain strategy is not purely a top-down planned process but also emerges from the learning, experimentation, and adaptations that occur in day-to-day supply chain operations — meaning that effective supply chain strategy requires both deliberate planning and the organizational capacity to recognize, learn from, and formalize successful emergent practices that arise from operational experience
Supply chain strategies should never be planned in advance
Emergent supply chain strategies are always superior to planned strategies

questionText: Analyze how "supply chain network effects" can create strategic competitive advantage:
options: Supply chain network effects are irrelevant to competitive strategy

In platform-based supply chains and logistics ecosystems, network effects occur when the value of the supply chain network increases as more participants join — creating a self-reinforcing competitive advantage where a supply chain platform that achieves critical mass becomes increasingly attractive to new participants, making it progressively harder for competitors to build a rival network of comparable value
Network effects only apply to social media companies
Supply chain network effects only affect transportation companies

questionText: A company is developing a supply chain strategy in response to growing demand for "circular economy" supply chains. Which supply chain capability is MOST critical to develop?
options: Increasing production capacity for new products

Reverse logistics capabilities — including product take-back systems, refurbishment and remanufacturing processes, material recovery networks, and closed-loop supply chain designs that return used products or materials back into the production process — supported by information systems that track product lifecycle and material flows
Reducing the number of products offered to simplify the supply chain
Increasing the speed of outbound delivery to customers

questionText: Evaluate which strategic supply chain investment would generate the GREATEST long-term competitive advantage for an Ethiopian manufacturing company competing in export markets:
options: Short-term price discounts to attract export buyers

Investment in supply chain capabilities that are difficult to replicate — including certified quality management systems, reliable cold chain or specialized logistics capabilities, strong relationships with international freight forwarders and customs brokers, digital supply chain visibility for export buyers, and sustainable sourcing practices — creating a supply chain foundation that supports sustainable export market growth
Copying the supply chain practices of competitor exporters
Minimizing all supply chain investment to maximize short-term profit

questionText: Which of the following BEST illustrates how supply chain strategy creates "barriers to imitation"?
options: Patenting supply chain processes to prevent competitor copying

Building supply chain capabilities that are deeply embedded in organizational culture, relationships, and accumulated learning — such as world-class supplier collaboration programs built over decades, proprietary logistics networks developed through years of investment, or supply chain talent pools nurtured through sustained development programs — which competitors cannot quickly replicate even if they understand what the company is doing
Keeping supply chain strategies secret from all external parties
Using proprietary software systems as the primary barrier to competitor imitation

questionText: A supply chain strategist must recommend how to manage the increasing complexity of a global supply chain serving 50 markets. Which strategic simplification approach is MOST effective?
options: Exiting all but the 5 largest markets to simplify the supply chain

Implementing supply chain segmentation — grouping markets with similar supply chain requirements into clusters served by standardized regional supply chain platforms, reducing complexity through intelligent standardization while maintaining the flexibility to customize where market differences genuinely create competitive value — supported by digital platforms that manage complexity efficiently
Using a single global supply chain design for all 50 markets without differentiation
Outsourcing all 50 market supply chains to local 3PL providers without strategic oversight

questionText: Critically analyze the strategic implication of the following statement: "The supply chain of the future will be autonomous."
options: Future supply chains will require no human involvement whatsoever

While increasing automation, AI, and digital technologies will enable higher levels of supply chain autonomy in routine operational decisions, human strategic judgment will remain essential for supply chain design, partner relationship management, ethical decision-making, navigating novel disruptions, and adapting strategy to changing competitive contexts — making the future supply chain a human-machine collaboration where technology handles routine complexity and humans focus on judgment-intensive strategic activities
Supply chain autonomy is technically impossible to achieve
Autonomous supply chains are only possible for simple, standardized product categories

questionText: Evaluate the strategic importance of "supply chain learning" for organizations pursuing supply chain excellence:
options: Supply chain learning is only important during the initial implementation of new systems

Supply chain learning — through systematic performance measurement, after-action reviews of disruptions and improvement initiatives, benchmarking, experimentation, and the development of organizational routines for capturing and applying supply chain knowledge — is a dynamic capability that enables continuous improvement, strategic adaptation, and the accumulation of hard-to-imitate supply chain expertise that compounds over time into significant competitive advantage
Supply chain learning is only relevant for academic institutions
Supply chain learning creates no competitive advantage because competitors can easily copy learned improvements

questionText: Which of the following BEST describes the strategic relationship between supply chain management and financial performance?
options: Supply chain management only affects operational costs with no impact on financial performance

Supply chain excellence directly drives financial performance through multiple mechanisms — including revenue protection through high service levels and supply continuity, cost efficiency through optimized procurement, inventory, and logistics, working capital optimization through inventory reduction and payment term management, and risk mitigation that protects earnings from disruption costs — making supply chain strategy a primary lever for improving enterprise financial performance
Supply chain management only affects cost, not revenue
Financial performance is determined solely by pricing and marketing strategy

questionText: A supply chain strategist identifies that the company's supply chain strategy is creating unintended negative social impacts in supplier communities. Which strategic response BEST reflects responsible supply chain leadership?
options: Ignoring the issue because it is the suppliers' responsibility to manage their own communities

Conducting a thorough supply chain social impact assessment, engaging affected communities and suppliers in dialogue, redesigning supply chain practices and sourcing requirements that are causing negative impacts, investing in supplier capability and community development programs, and transparently reporting on progress — treating responsible supply chain management as a strategic priority rather than a compliance exercise
Immediately terminating relationships with all suppliers in affected communities
Issuing a public statement about the company's commitment to responsible sourcing without changing supply chain practices

questionText: Which of the following MOST accurately captures the evolution of supply chain strategic thinking over the past three decades?
options: Supply chain thinking has remained unchanged since the 1990s

Supply chain strategic thinking has evolved from a narrow focus on logistics cost reduction to recognition of supply chains as strategic assets; from linear chain models to complex networked ecosystems; from efficiency optimization to balancing efficiency with resilience, agility, and sustainability; from company-centric to supply chain-wide optimization; and increasingly toward digitally-enabled, customer-centric, and purpose-driven supply chain strategies
Supply chain strategic thinking has only changed due to technology developments
Supply chain strategic thinking has evolved from complex to simple approaches

questionText: Analyze how a company should use "supply chain benchmarking" strategically rather than merely operationally:
options: Benchmarking should only be used to compare costs with competitors

Strategic benchmarking uses supply chain performance comparisons not just to identify operational gaps but to generate strategic insights — understanding how best-in-class supply chains achieve their performance, what capabilities and investments underlie their advantage, which benchmarking insights apply to the company's strategic context, and how closing identified gaps would translate into competitive differentiation — using benchmarking as an input to strategic planning rather than just operational improvement
Benchmarking should only be conducted with direct competitors
Benchmarking is only valuable for large multinational companies

questionText: Which of the following BEST evaluates the role of "supply chain culture" in achieving strategic supply chain excellence?
options: Culture is irrelevant to supply chain performance — only processes and technology matter

Supply chain culture — the shared values, beliefs, behaviors, and norms that shape how supply chain professionals make decisions and interact with partners — is a foundational determinant of supply chain excellence; a culture of continuous improvement, customer focus, collaboration, transparency, and accountability creates the organizational environment in which supply chain strategies are effectively executed and supply chain capabilities continuously developed
Supply chain culture only matters for large organizations
Supply chain culture is solely the responsibility of the HR department

questionText: A final-year logistics and supply chain management student is preparing for a career in strategic supply chain management in Ethiopia. Which strategic supply chain challenge should they be MOST prepared to address in their career?
options: Managing stable supply chains in developed market contexts

Building supply chain capabilities that drive Ethiopia's economic development — navigating infrastructure development phases, supporting industrial park growth, managing the complexity of integrating Ethiopian supply chains into global value chains, leveraging East Africa's regional integration opportunities, addressing supply chain sustainability challenges, and leading digital supply chain transformation in an emerging market context where supply chain excellence can directly contribute to national competitiveness and economic inclusion
Replicating supply chain models from developed countries without adaptation
Focusing exclusively on cost reduction in existing supply chain operations
